You are a professional biblical lexicographer fluent in Spanish. Translate the following English lexicon entry into Spanish.

Lemma: H6213a

ENGLISH GLOSSES TO TRANSLATE:
  Terse gloss: "Do, perform, act; make, construct; be done (Niphal); produce, yield; work, labor"
  Readable gloss: "The great all-purpose Hebrew verb of action, appearing over 2,600 times. Like English 'do' and 'make' combined, it covers everything from God creating the heavens to a farmer tending his field. Its semantic range stretches from the divine—'your Maker' as a title for God (Job 4:17)—to the agricultural, where a vineyard 'produces' wild grapes (Isa 5:2). The Niphal passive allows events to simply 'be done' without naming an agent, a construction favored in legal and narrative contexts. Arabic preserves a similar split between faʿala (do) and ṣanaʿa (make), hinting that Hebrew merged two Proto-Semitic roots into one workhorse verb."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "do, perform, act"
    Enriched: The default Qal sense: to do, perform, carry out an action or command. With 2,383 occurrences, this covers obedience ('Noah did all that God commanded,' Gen 6:22), wrongdoing ('he did evil,' Gen 38:10), and every kind of purposeful activity. Spanish 'hizo' and German 'tat' match its generality perfectly.
    Existing Spanish translations: hizo
  Sense 2: "make, construct, fabricate"
    Enriched: To make, build, or construct a physical object. Concentrated in Exodus 25-40 where the tabernacle furnishings are fashioned: 'you shall make a mercy seat' (Exod 25:17). Spanish 'harás' and German 'machen' both distinguish this constructive sense from mere doing, paralleling the English make/do split.
    Existing Spanish translations: Y-harás, y-harás
  Sense 3: "be done, be made (Niphal)"
    Enriched: Niphal passive: to be done or be made, removing the agent from view. Genesis 20:9 asks 'what have you done to us?' using a form that emphasizes the deed over the doer. French 'être fait' and Spanish 'se hará' capture this impersonal construction common in legal contexts and divine pronouncements (Gen 22:16).
    Existing Spanish translations: hiciste, les-será-hecho, se-hará, se-haría, será-hecho
  Sense 4: "Maker, Creator"
    Enriched: Participial substantive: Maker or Creator as a title. Job 4:17 asks 'shall a man be more pure than his Maker?' where the participle becomes a divine name. Spanish 'El que hizo' and English 'his Maker' show this shift from verb to title, a usage concentrated in Job and the Psalms (Ps 136:4; Job 31:15; 40:19).
    Existing Spanish translations: Al-que-hace, Al-que-hizo, El-que-hizo, a-Hacedor-su, el-hacedor-de, el-que-lo-hizo, hace, hacedor-de, lo-hizo, más-que-su-Hacedor, su-Hacedor
  Sense 5: "produce, yield fruit"
    Enriched: To produce or yield fruit and crops, a specialized agricultural sense. Isaiah 5:2-10's vineyard parable uses it repeatedly—the vine was expected to 'produce' good grapes but 'made' wild ones instead. Spanish 'producirá' distinguishes this from generic 'hacer,' revealing a semantic narrowing toward natural fertility.
    Existing Spanish translations: más-pude-hacer, para-producir, producirá, producirán
  Sense 6: "work, labor, toil"
    Enriched: To work, labor, or toil at a task or occupation over sustained time. Ruth 2:19 asks 'where did you work today?' and Nehemiah 4:6 describes builders who 'worked' with determination. Swahili 'kufanya kazi' (do work) and Spanish 'trabajar' capture the emphasis on effort and employment rather than a single completed act.
    Existing Spanish translations: cuando-obra, para-hacer, trabajar, trabajaste, trabajó
